And being looked at has a cost. In an experiment, women whose bodies were stared at solved fewer math problems afterward: just under 5 of 12, versus about 6. Men's scores didn't drop.

So the first glance is fast. The stare is a choice. Look at her face.

You wait for them to text first. Here's what that costs you. 💌

Let's simulate it: ten people on each side. Everyone secretly ranks everyone. One side asks. The other side holds on to the best offer so far. Round after round, until everyone is matched.

The askers got their number two on average. The ones who waited: number five.

Swap the sides, and it flips. The math is proven: in this model, asking never makes you worse off.

In this model, asking never makes you worse off. It's a proven theorem. Real dating is messier, of course. But the lesson holds: send the first message.

Send the first message. Then save this. 🔖

You think attractive people are mean. It's a statistics trick. 🎲

Let's simulate it: 400 people. Looks and kindness are totally random, no link at all.

Now you only date people who are attractive enough, kind enough, or both. Among the ones left, the better looking they are, the meaner they get.

Because the mean and plain ones never made your list. So the hot ones you meet don't need to be nice to get there.

It's called Berkson's paradox. It's not that hot people are mean. It's who you filtered out.

Send this to someone who dates jerks. 👇

You settled too early. Or you waited too long. There's a rule for that. 🃏

Say you'll date ten people, one after another. Once you pass on someone, they're gone. So when do you commit?

The math says: skip the first 37%. Just look. Then pick the first one who beats them all.

We simulated 1,000 love lives, ten dates each. The rule found the very best one 40% of the time. Committing to the first date, or picking at random: only about 10%.

Real life is messier. People can say no, and you never know how many you'll meet. But the lesson holds: explore first. Then commit.
